spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The mathematical work is the normalization of critical-line exponents as (1−η)/6: it turns improvements over the classical 1/6 into directly comparable saving parameters. In that coordinate, moving from η=1/28 with an essentially optimal A4 bound to η=1/14 with an essentially optimal A6 bound exactly doubles the saving, while the A5 comparison records a historically obstructed intermediate case.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The remark writes 9/56=(1−1/28)/6 for the Bombieri–Iwaniec result based on an essentially optimal A4(δ,Hδ) bound and 13/84=(1−1/14)/6 for the result based on an essentially optimal A6(δ,Hδ) bound. It therefore identifies the latter as twice the improvement over 1/6. It also records 17/108=(1−1/18)/6 from an A5 input and says 11/70=(1−2/35)/6 was blocked at the time by cases with α near 23/54.
directed.conceptual_reading: Writing every exponent as a deficit from the same baseline isolates the gain supplied by the moment estimate. The coordinate η compresses the comparison: the theorem exponents differ, but their methodological progress is read from the size of the removed fraction rather than from the raw rational numbers.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The bridge objects are the first-spacing quantities A4, A5, and A6 and the normalized saving parameter η in (1−η)/6. The displayed identities translate improvements in those moment inputs into critical-line exponent savings and make the doubling claim arithmetically transparent.
directed.boundary_or_failure: This span compares the consequences of essentially optimal moment bounds; it does not derive those bounds or establish the transfer from each A_r estimate to its zeta exponent. The unrealized 11/70 value is explicitly limited by a difficult α-range, so it is not presented as an achieved bound.
directed.uncertainty: The PDF text layer carries formula risk, but the rational identities and comparative prose are legible. The account of the α≈23/54 obstruction is a source-authored historical statement, not independently verified within this unit.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The unit turns a scale-restricted estimate into a reusable exponent-pair statement by making the missing regimes explicit. For M above the direct range, it preserves the sum under a parameter rescaling, handles extreme scales with the classical (1/2,1/2) pair, and sends the intermediate range through Poisson and partial summation to a dual length M′≈T/M where the original estimate applies.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: From (5.1) the source states that (ε+13/84, ε+55/84) is an exponent pair, corresponding to |S|≪(T/M)^(13/84+ε) M^(55/84+ε)=M^(1/2)T^(13/84+ε). It identifies two weaker requirements still to be handled: M may exceed T^(1/2), and the sum and phase may be available only on a proper subinterval. For the first, it rescales c,F,T to c1=TM^(−2)c, F1=TM^(−2)F, T1=M² without changing S; uses (1/2,1/2) when M≥T^(9/10); and converts T^(1/2)<M<T^(9/10) by Poisson and partial summation to M′≈T/M, T′≈T in the direct scale range.
directed.conceptual_reading: An exponent pair is functioning as a portable summary of a bound, but portability requires closure under changes of scale. The proof strategy partitions the parameter space, uses a harmless reparameterization where possible, a coarse fallback at the extreme, and duality in the middle. The asserted fixed-point behavior under the B-process explains why dualization returns the same exponent-pair claim rather than a different target.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The bridge is the passage from the original pair of scale variables (M,T) to either the unchanged-sum representation with T1=M² or the dual representation (M′,T′) with M′≈T/M. Poisson summation, partial summation, and the B-process connect the intermediate large-M sum to the range governed by (5.1); the exponent pair packages the resulting estimate independently of a single scale presentation.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The Poisson/B-process conversion is cited rather than proved, and the extreme regime relies on the already known pair (1/2,1/2). This unit only identifies the proper-subinterval problem (b); its extension and restriction argument is not supplied here. Thus the exponent-pair generalization depends on external exponent-pair hypotheses and later localization work.
directed.uncertainty: Several fraction glyphs in the scale and B-process formulas are visibly degraded by extraction. The qualitative claims, the exponents 13/84 and 55/84, the substitutions, and M′≈T/M are legible; the damaged displayed B-formula is not reconstructed beyond the source's stated fixed-point role.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The useful intermediate object is a global phase extension f1 that agrees with the given phase on [a,b] but belongs to the derivative class required by exponent-pair theory on [M/2,M]. A monomial derivative model supplies the main extension and a small polynomial correction enforces matching; a restriction lemma then returns to the original subinterval at only logarithmic cost.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Assuming f′ on [a,b] has the required monomial approximation yx^(−s), the source extends beyond b by taking f1(x)=y∫_b^x u^(−s)du+a0+a1x+⋯+aP x^P. It states that the coefficients can be chosen for matching at b and are small enough that the required derivative conditions through order P persist on [a,M]. A similar construction extends to the left, producing a phase on [M/2,M]; Sargos's lemma 2.1 then restricts the resulting estimate to the original interval with an O(log M) loss.
directed.conceptual_reading: The construction is an interface adapter between local data and a theorem whose hypotheses are global on a dyadic interval. It preserves the phase where the target sum lives, controls what is added outside that interval through derivative bounds, and separates extension from localization. The logarithmic loss is the explicit price for moving through this global representation.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The bridge object is f1: its integral term continues the monomial model for f′, while the polynomial correction handles boundary matching without destroying the derivative class. Agreement on [a,b] preserves the original summands, and the interval-restriction lemma transfers the full-dyadic estimate back to [a,b].
directed.boundary_or_failure: The method assumes the original phase already satisfies the exponent-pair derivative conditions and possesses the stated monomial approximation. Smallness of the correction coefficients and preservation of all required derivatives are asserted from the cited condition rather than demonstrated here; the final localization also depends on an external lemma and incurs O(log M).
directed.uncertainty: The extraction damages some derivative superscripts and the displayed integral typography, but the extension mechanism and logarithmic loss are readable. The precise coefficient-matching system and the cited derivative condition are not reproduced in this span, so their detailed sufficiency remains context-dependent.
